hops.title: Your fingernail versus a regrowing axon
hops.text: Look at the pale tip of one fingernail. In a 2010 study of 22 healthy young adults, fingernails grew an average of 3.47 millimetres a month, a little over a tenth of a millimetre a day, and the little fingernail grew more slowly than the rest. Toenails managed 1.62 millimetres a month. A regrowing axon in a human nerve advances about a millimetre a day, nearly nine times as fast as a fingernail, though the pace varies with the nerve and the injury. Brisk, by the standards of your body. Now trace a line from your collarbone to your fingertips, and imagine covering it at that pace.

sources.citation: Yaemsiri S, Hou N, Slining MM, He K (2010). Growth rate of human fingernails and toenails in healthy American young adults. J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 24(4):420-423.
Gordon T (2020). Peripheral nerve regeneration and muscle reinnervation. Int J Mol Sci 21(22):8652.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A hand resting on a wooden desk next to a brass magnifying glass, showing the pale tips of the fingernails.
image.caption: A regrowing human axon outpaces a fingernail nearly ninefold, and still needs months to cross an arm.

hops.title: The crayfish axons that would not fall apart
hops.text: In ordinary mice, most axons beyond a cut in the sciatic nerve break apart within about two days. In 1967, Ronald Hoy, George Bittner and Donald Kennedy cut crayfish motor axons and found something else entirely. The pieces cut off from their cell bodies stayed electrically excitable, and kept storing and releasing normal amounts of transmitter, for more than 100 days. Their evidence also suggested that the regrowing end fused with its surviving stump. Later work found the cut-off pieces of crayfish giant axons still viable after more than seven months. Two days in a mouse; more than seven months in a crayfish.

sources.citation: Beirowski B, Adalbert R, Wagner D, et al. (2005). The progressive nature of Wallerian degeneration in wild-type and slow Wallerian degeneration (WldS) nerves. BMC Neurosci 6:6.
Hoy RR, Bittner GD, Kennedy D (1967). Regeneration in crustacean motoneurons: evidence for axonal fusion. Science 156(3772):251-252.

Tanner SL, Storm EE, Bittner GD (1995). Maintenance and degradation of proteins in intact and severed axons: implications for the mechanisms of long-term survival of anucleate crayfish axons. J Neurosci 15(1 Pt 2):540-548.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A reddish-brown freshwater crayfish resting on smooth river stones in clear shallow water with one claw raised.
image.caption: Cut-off crayfish motor axons carry signals when stimulated months later; most distal mouse sciatic axons fragment within about two days.

hops.title: Crocodile tears at the dinner table
hops.text: A facial nerve can grow back and still deliver its messages to the wrong place. After a facial nerve injury such as Bell palsy, regenerating autonomic fibres meant for the salivary glands can stray into pathways that lead to the tear gland instead. Some time after the injury, chewing or smelling food makes the eye on that side tear. The condition is also called Bogorad syndrome, after the Russian neuropathologist F. A. Bogorad, and crocodile tears syndrome, after the old belief that crocodiles weep as they eat. The axons did regrow. They connected the signal for salivating to the wrong gland.

sources.citation: Tripathy K, Arsiwalla T (2025). Crocodile Tears Syndrome. StatPearls. Treasure Island (FL): StatPearls Publishing.
McCoy FJ, Goodman RC (1979). The crocodile tear syndrome. Plast Reconstr Surg 63(1):58-62.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A polite green crocodile sitting at a wooden cafe table with a napkin and a lemon tart, shedding one big tear.
image.caption: When regrowing salivary fibres wire into the tear gland, the smell of dinner brings tears.
